For generic coefficients the response is nonstationary and depends on both the duration and temporal location of the measurement. The spectrum, which is the resulting excitation rate as a function of the energy level difference in the detector, is obtained numerically. It shows discernable differences with the usual massive thermal spectrum for dimensionless coefficients on the order of $10^{-7}$. Experimental implications of the result are discussed. As an alternative viewpoint, we place Lorentz violation in the point-particle sector, derive the exact trajectory generated by a constant electric field, and study the proper-time Fourier response of a conventional scalar wave along the modified trajectory.

papers.title: Hearsay: Who Can Audit the Record a Deployed Agent Harness Writes?
papers.abstract: The record of an agent's run is written by the harness that drives the agent. When the run is later disputed, the auditor was not there and has only this record. We ask whether someone who was not there can check the record, and what decides the answer. It depends on who wrote what a check can rely on: if the harness wrote all of it, the record is only the harness's own word, and we call it hearsay. We build Hearsay, a benchmark that examines the record and not the task: five harnesses run fourteen tasks, model examiners from three vendors and a human panel read the records and answer questions about the runs, and every passage they cite is labelled mechanically by who wrote it. We also audit what is deployed: in all sixteen frameworks, the harness is the only writer. With one writer, readers can name the fault from the record, in up to nine runs in ten, but they cannot check the record. The model examiners claim corroboration for 18 to 55 points more of their evidence than the labels support, a gap we then predicted for runs driven by another vendor's model and found again. And the best of them notices only half of the alterations we make to a record, while the two that name the fault most often cannot tell what a harness left out. With a second writer, the record can be checked. Our sandbox keeps a ledger of what passes between harness and model, and reading the ledger against the record in both directions shows what the record leaves out and what it adds. We test this as an auditor would use it, on one unseen record at a time. On runs driven by a third vendor's model, with every rule committed before the records existed, it reports 64 of 66 alterations and flags none of 84 clean records. On held-out records in five formats it reports 109 of 115. What makes a record evidence is a second writer, not a better reader.

papers.title: Elastic Selective Spectral Hybrids for Train-Once, Export-Many Budgeted Inference
papers.abstract: Deploying a language model under different computing and latency budgets calls for compact models with different quality-cost trade-offs. Towards this end, elastic spectral state space models provide ordered and temporally decomposed channels that can be truncated, but they are associated with linear time-invariant filters that cannot selectively preserve relevant past information or forget irrelevant information as the context evolves. To address this, we introduce the Elastic Selective Spectral Hybrid (ESSH), which realizes each Hankel spectral channel as an independent recurrent unit using fitted damped rotation modes. It also features an input-dependent decay and write/read gates that make temporal retention and state update input-dependent while preserving channel-wise truncation and a structured recurrence for efficient execution. ESSH combines these selective spectral mixers with sliding-window attention and jointly trains multiple capacities by reducing spectral-channel count and feed-forward width at different rates through a two-rate capacity map with full-model distillation. The resulting models support chunked parallel training and fused recurrent decoding while avoiding computation for discarded channels. At full capacity, ESSH achieves language-modeling quality comparable to similarly sized independently trained models, while smaller exports exhibit a smooth quality-cost trade-off. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework using language understanding, retrieval, cross-domain text, and DNA experiments, by assessing quality retention and the trade-off against independently trained and elastic baselines. At the 1.53B model configuration, fused batch-one decoding takes 1.37 ms per token on a B300, providing a 2.14-2.80x speedup over the tested Mamba-2 and Mamba-3 implementations and 3.03x over Transformer++ at matched parameter counts.

papers.title: Cost-Efficient LLM Evaluation: A Framework for Narrow Confidence Intervals Under Fixed Budgets
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasingly important role in both academic research and industry. Reliable evaluation helps researchers understand model capabilities and assess progress during model development. However, evaluation can be costly, and researchers often need to assess performance within a fixed budget. Because model outputs can vary across runs, this budget must be allocated between testing different tasks and repeating selected tasks. A confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty in the resulting performance estimate. Obtaining narrower intervals at the same confidence level and evaluation cost provides a more precise assessment of model performance, helping researchers draw clearer conclusions from limited observations. We introduce a framework that allocates a fixed evaluation budget across tasks and repeated runs, with or without full task coverage. The framework then uses disagreements between runs on the same task to bound estimation error, allowing narrower confidence intervals at the same confidence level when the sampled repeats show little variability. When repeated runs on each task yield the same outcome, we prove that our framework achieves the fastest theoretically possible rates for narrowing confidence intervals in the worst case as the number of tasks and the budget for repeats grow. We establish matching lower bounds both when every task must be covered and when tasks may be skipped, even for evaluators who use earlier results to decide which run to carry out next. On LiveCodeBench, our framework yielded narrower confidence intervals on average than uniform random sampling in 15 of 16 model configurations, with a median width reduction of 30.6% at the same confidence level and the same budget of 1,100 outputs per configuration.

papers.title: Who Is Behind the Harness? Verifying Model Identity in Coding Agents through Behavioral Fingerprinting
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly operate through coding-agent harnesses that inspect repositories, invoke tools, and modify files. Substituting the model behind such an agent can therefore change security-relevant decisions, including whether it verifies changes or recovers safely from failures. Existing LLM fingerprints largely infer identity from direct text or token distributions. In coding agents, these signals are mediated by system instructions, controller logic, tools, and execution feedback, limiting their transfer. We present LIDAR (LLM Identification from Decisions and Actions at Runtime), an active black-box fingerprinting method for coding-agent execution. Three coding probe pairs expose post-edit verification, transient-failure recovery, and specification--test conflict resolution under controlled changes. LIDAR represents the resulting trajectories with complementary instance-level and distribution-level features and compares them with clean references using a lightweight probabilistic identifier. It requires no access to model weights, logits, or provider internals. We evaluate 24 models from eight families on OpenCode, OpenHands, and mini-swe-agent, fitting separate references for each harness. Closed-set Top-1 accuracy ranges from 91.39\% to 98.89\% across the three harnesses, exceeding all three baselines in each setting. When the audit also includes unregistered models from the same families, balanced accuracy ranges from 79.58\% to 80.42\%. These results show that agent execution behavior provides model-identity evidence beyond final outputs.

papers.title: When Does Reallocating a Sampling Budget Pay? Instance-wise Allocation for Neural Routing Solvers
papers.abstract: Neural routing solvers sample many solutions per instance and keep the best, with the same number of samples for every instance. We measure how much a non-uniform split of the same total budget is worth and which property of a workload decides it. Best-of-k curves estimated by averaging random orderings of stored samples overstate the gain, and deciding on one half of the samples while evaluating on the other understates it; we use exact best-of-k curves, a U-statistic over all orderings. For three pretrained solvers (POMO, the Attention Model and Sym-NCO) on the traveling salesman problem, reallocation reduces the total optimality gap by at most 2.5% on the training distribution, so uniform allocation is close to optimal there. On workloads that mix in out-of-distribution instances it reduces the gap by 11.8-13.3% (1.1-1.8% of tour length) for the two solvers that degrade under the shift, and almost nothing for the one that does not. Across two heterogeneity mechanisms, three solvers, two confirmation collections and budgets of 25 to 200 samples per instance, the gain is predicted by the spread of difficulty within a workload, not its average. Allocating on a power-law curve fitted to twenty charged probe samples per instance recovers 88-93% of the uncharged optimum; successive halving does worse. A 2-opt local search, however, removes most of the gap at negligible cost, after which reallocation adds a few hundredths of a percent of tour length.

papers.title: Asymptotic quasi--local structure induced by Magnetic field
papers.abstract: We introduce a magnetic coherent--state frame over the Landau levels of the two--dimensional Landau Hamiltonian, indexed by a discrete metric space combining spatial and energy degrees of freedom. Although overcomplete, the frame is almost--orthogonal, and we use it to endow the CAR $C^*$--algebra over the one--particle Hilbert space with an \emph{asymptotic quasi--local} (AQL) structure, in which graded commutators of observables localized on disjoint index sets decay exponentially rather than vanish exactly. By means of a family of conditional expectations onto the resulting local subalgebras, we construct a Fréchet $*$--subalgebra of almost--local observables, invariant under the discrete group of lattice translations, which act on it by continuous automorphisms. For the full continuous group of magnetic translations we establish a quantitative control on how local observables spread through this almost--local algebra, and we show that this control {exhibits the compatibility of the AQL structure with graded asymptotic abelianness under the entire continuous translation group. The dependence on the volume of the localization regions of the constants in the AQL bound is left as an open problem.} The results provide a discrete--continuum dictionary intended as the starting point for extending Lieb--Robinson--type techniques from lattice systems to interacting continuum electrons in a magnetic field.

papers.title: Strong Selective and List-Decoding Direct Product Theorems for Quantum Query Complexity
papers.abstract: Quantum strong direct-product theorems for specific functions have been known for nearly two decades. These have been extended to general results for function computation and state generation. The proofs of these results use a version of the multiplicative adversary method that does not naturally extend to relations. Standard strong direct-product theorems apply when algorithms must correctly answer every given question. Prior work extended them to equivalent threshold direct-product theorems, which require answers to all questions but only require that most answers are correct. We focus on two further generalizations. Strong selective direct-products apply to algorithms that adaptively choose, based on what they learn from queries, which questions from a large list to answer. This generalization is relational and useful for proving time-space tradeoffs. We prove a quantum strong selective direct-product theorem for all functions using a relational formulation of the multiplicative adversary method by Jeffery and Zur which we prove, via an equivalent formulation, satisfies a strong selective direct product property and captures any query lower bound for functions proven by negative-weights adversaries. The second generalization is list-decoding direct product problems introduced by Ben-David and Blais for classical query complexity. These allow an algorithm to produce a large list of possible output vectors such that one of them is fully correct. They proved that such theorems hold for randomized complexity of all Boolean functions. We prove a quantum analogue of this theorem for all partial Boolean-valued functions. We show that strong list-decoding direct-product theorems are implied by a special case of multiplicative adversaries which we show, via a new reduction, can be obtained from negative-weights adversaries for any Boolean-valued function.

papers.title: Repeated averaging on random $d$-regular graphs
papers.abstract: Repeated averaging on graphs is a natural prototype of local stochastic exchange, modeling consensus formation, information spreading, and wealth redistribution. Its convergence has attracted longstanding interest, from Bourgain's complete-graph $L^1$ cutoff question in the 1980s (answered in recent years by Chatterjee, Diaconis, Sly, and Zhang) to the systematic study of Aldous and Lanoue. Towards the still outstanding and widely asked $L^1$ cutoff question on general graphs, we establish a criterion for $L^1$ cutoff based on size-biased sampling. We then prove $L^1$ cutoff with a Gaussian profile on random $d$-regular graphs, for any $d\ge 3$ and uniformly over starting vertices. Remarkably, although the expected mass profile agrees exactly with the corresponding random walk distribution, cutoff occurs strictly later than both the random walk cutoff time and the universal lower bound attained on complete graphs, revealing an unexpected entropy gap. Our methods are robust, involving ideas of polymer representations, random geometry, universal-cover lifting, and adaptive revealing. We expect them to be applicable to repeated averaging and similar interacting systems with random exchange rules on a wide range of graphs.

papers.title: FPT Isomorphism Test for $F$-Free Tournaments
papers.abstract: We show that isomorphism of $F$-free tournaments can be solved in FPT time $f(k) \cdot n^{O(1)}$, where $k$ denotes the size of $F$, and $n$ denotes the size of the input tournaments. Our result extends on a previous FPT isomorphism test for tournaments of bounded twin-width [Grohe, Neuen 2024], as well as XP isomorphism tests parameterized by the VC dimension or the chromatic number [Raßmann, Schweitzer 2026]. It also implies that every non-trivial hereditary class of tournaments admits a polynomial-time isomorphism test. Our algorithm builds on a combination of spectral, geometric, combinatorial and group-theoretic tools.

papers.title: Circuit Hypernetworks for Quantum-Augmented Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Improving pretrained language models with limited adaptation data calls for computational modules that are both effective and scalable. Parameterized quantum circuits offer expressive transformations for language modeling, yet existing quantum-enhanced language models apply the same predefined circuit design to every token in an input sequence, regardless of its content. This limitation is particularly acute in masked-diffusion language models, where token representations evolve across iterative denoising steps while the circuit design remains fixed. We introduce HyperQ, a quantum-augmented masked-diffusion language model that dynamically synthesizes token-specific quantum circuits. Built upon an IQP-inspired architecture, HyperQ employs a lightweight circuit hypernetwork to generate rotation angles and measurement bases conditioned on each token's hidden state. The resulting quantum expectation values are projected back into the frozen language-model backbone through a residual connection. To support wider quantum registers, HyperQ bounds circuit interaction degree, maintaining per-qubit gradient scale and readout cost independent of register width. Across six zero-shot benchmarks, scaling HyperQ from 16 to 64 qubits improves average accuracy from 47.65 to 54.30, surpassing the frozen backbone's 49.59 by 4.71 points while using only one tenth of the fine-tuning data used by classical baselines. We further execute the generated circuits on an IBM 156-qubit superconducting quantum processor, demonstrating their feasibility on physical quantum hardware.

papers.title: WorkWorlds: Evaluating Agents in a Company Built Before the Task
papers.abstract: Many knowledge work benchmarks are built around single tasks, where the context and files for each task are selected concurrently or after task definition. Research has argued that this construction method does not reflect real workplace work, yet the impact has never been measured under controlled conditions. To compare the two constructions under controlled conditions, we introduce WorkWorlds, an infrastructure that modularizes company components into revision, date, and employee seat to be separately adjusted. Using historical data donated by a real company, we reconstructed a pharmaceutical company, PharmaCo. Two experts with over ten years of industry experience each wrote eight tasks based on real events that occurred at the company, and each independently constructed a task-specific environment for every task. Across 192 controlled evaluations, when the agent was switched from the task-specific environment to all the materials truly visible to the employee, evidence access dropped from 90.4 percent to 72.8 percent, and the criterion pass rate dropped from 76.7 percent to 68.0 percent. However, in cases where the agent found the required evidence, the pass rates under both conditions were almost identical. Furthermore, switching between the environments built by the two experts for the same task resulted in an average pass rate difference of 6.6 percentage points. The three agents also gained by different amounts, which changed the gaps between them. We argue that benchmarks should report how environment materials were selected and, if possible, they should test agent score changes after changing the environment builder.

papers.title: Distill What You Trust: Reliability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation allows a student to learn from complementary specialists on its own trajectories. Domain-routed approaches, however, select one teacher per example and keep it fixed throughout the response. This design both depends on domain labels that mixed training corpora often lack and cannot adapt teacher selection when the expertise required changes within a trajectory. We observe that each specialist deviates more from a shared reference on in-domain prompts than on out-of-domain prompts, on average. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{TrustMOPD}, which replaces example-level teacher selection with label-free, token-level supervision allocation. At each student-generated prefix, TrustMOPD measures this displacement in next-token preferences, calibrates its magnitude across teachers, and uses the resulting scores as proxies for local reliability to weight teacher-specific distillation losses. Evaluated across mathematics, code, and instruction following, TrustMOPD closes 91.5\% and 98.0\% of the overall-score gap between the initial student and oracle-routed teachers when trained on \textsc{SingleCap} and \textsc{MultiCap}, respectively, compared with 54.4\% and 54.5\% for the strongest label-free baseline in each setting. On \textsc{SingleCap}, it approaches label-based MOPD without using domain labels. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunjie279/TrustMOPD-.

papers.title: Multiset Colorings of Random Graphs Across Density Regimes
papers.abstract: We show that almost every graph admits a partition of its vertex set into three parts such that no two adjacent vertices have the same number of neighbors in each of the three parts. Equivalently, for $G\sim G(n,1/2)$, $χ_m(G)\le3$ with high probability, improving the previously known bound of five. Here $χ_m(G)$ denotes the multiset chromatic number of $G$, the minimum number of parts in a vertex partition whose neighbor-count vectors distinguish every pair of adjacent vertices. In fact, the three-part bound holds for every fixed $0.185<p<0.509$. More generally, for every fixed $p\in(0,1)$, $G\sim G(n,p)$ satisfies $χ_m(G)\le4$ with high probability. These results are obtained by converting the unresolved edges of a carefully chosen initial partition into hyperplanes of a Boolean cube and applying the Linial--Radhakrishnan theory of essential covers. We also determine how $χ_m(G)$ grows when the graph is polynomially close to complete. For every fixed $β\in(0,1)$ and $G\sim G\!\left(n,1-n^{-(1-β)}\right)$, with high probability $\frac{2}β\le χ_m(G)\le \left\lfloor\frac{2}β\right\rfloor+5$. Thus $χ_m(G)=2/β+O(1)$. The lower bound is spectral, while the upper bound follows from multinomial anti-concentration and the Lov'asz Local Lemma.

papers.title: Free Boundary Propagation of a Thin-Film Equation with Nonlinear Diffusion: Scale-Consistent Methods for Optimal Results
papers.abstract: We investigate the free boundary propagation of a non-linear degenerate parabolic problem with both fourth and second order non-linearities, which may be used to model viscous thin-film flow in the regime of weak slippage with an additional contributions from a singular disjoining pressure brought forth by inter-molecular forces. By carefully treating the individual scaling behaviors of the non-linearities, we obtain asymptotically optimal upper and lower bounds on the rate of forward support propagation. These rates show that the fourth-order operator dominates the propagation rate on short time scales, but the long-term rate of propagation is controlled by the second-order operator. We estimate further the time at which this trade-off in propagation rate occurs. Lastly, we examine sufficient conditions to ensure that the free boundary does not immediately advance in a given direction, leading to a detailed picture of how the competition between the second/fourth-order operators influence the free boundary dynamics of solutions.

papers.title: The "Rough" HAR Model
papers.abstract: This paper proposes discrete-time approximations to rough continuous-time models of realized variance (RV). The leading rough models can be viewed as autoregressive processes driven by fractional Gaussian noise. We show that the Wold representation of this noise concentrates its dependence at the first lag when the Hurst parameter is below one half. Augmenting the autoregressive (AR) and heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) models with a first-order moving-average (MA(1)) component therefore approximates the roughness, and the MA coefficient maps almost linearly into the Hurst parameter. We refer to these extensions as the "rough" AR and "rough" HAR models. Estimating them on the log RV of ten ETFs, we find negative MA coefficients for every asset, and the implied Hurst parameters align closely with the estimates from the continuous-time models. In the HAR literature, the negative MA(1) component is a significant feature that has been largely overlooked. In out-of-sample comparisons, the "rough" models outperform their classical counterparts for nearly every asset and horizon, with the largest gains at short horizons, and their accuracy is comparable to that of the rough continuous-time models but much easier to estimate by standard off-the-shelf software.

papers.title: On the parametric and semiparametric Fisher information matrix for non-zero mean stationary spherical invariant random processes
papers.abstract: The classical Whittle formula provides a closed-form expression for the asymptotic Fisher information matrix (FIM) rate of multidimensional, real-valued, zero-mean, purely nondeterministic stationary Gaussian processes (GPs), expressed in terms of their parameterized spectra within a maximum-likelihood framework. However, the Gaussian assumption underlying this result restricts its applicability to many real-world signals exhibiting heavy-tailed or non-Gaussian behavior. In this paper, we extend Whittle's result to multidimensional, real-valued stationary compound Gaussian processes (CGPs) with arbitrary mean, under a unified framework encompassing fully known, parameterized, and completely unknown density generators. Building upon the Slepian-Bangs formula for $n$ consecutive observations and extending it to the semiparametric setting, we leverage the asymptotic properties of block Toeplitz matrices to obtain a closed-form spectral-domain expression for the asymptotic FIM rate. The resulting expression, common to all density generator families, generalizes the standard zero-mean Gaussian formula by incorporating a distribution-dependent contribution associated with the nonzero mean, and an additional covariance term that is invariant to the choice of non-Gaussian distribution. This extension enables efficient and theoretically grounded performance analysis for heavy-tailed signal processing applications.

papers.title: Distilling a Geospatial Foundation Model into Compact Surface-Water Segmenters
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models segment surface water accurately, but their size limits deployment on edge hardware. Therefore, we distill a 300-million-parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher, fine-tuned on the 252 hand-labeled Sen1Floods11 training images, into compact student models. The teacher labels 2,500 Sentinel-2 images around flood alerts and supervises the students via its labels and probability maps, without manual annotation. A 0.7-million-parameter EfficientViT-B0 student achieves the teacher's accuracy in water intersection over union (IoU) on WorldFloods-v2, STURM-Flood and 97 held-back WorldFloods events. Unlike prior work, we evaluate every model on four test sets from three public datasets and on two new dry-scene sets. Controlled comparisons show that teacher labels achieve human-level annotation quality for student training on the same images. The teacher's probability maps account for much of its value, and the full pipeline adds 5.7 IoU points on the held-back events over training on hand labels alone. All students, with parameter counts ranging from about 1,000 to 32.5 million, perform within 2 IoU points of the teacher on WorldFloods-v2 and STURM-Flood. On a Jetson Xavier NX, the main student runs as a 1.6-megabyte mixed 8-bit integer and 16-bit floating-point engine at 4.9 milliseconds per 512-by-512 image, and a 12,230-parameter student runs in full 8-bit integer format within 0.5 IoU points of its 32-bit version. The main student outperforms a fixed water index by 11.5 IoU points on the held-back events and raises false alarms on under 10\% rather than 57.0\% of water-free windows, as unattended use requires.

papers.title: Ischemic Stroke Segmentation and Net Water Uptake Quantification on Multicenter Non-Contrast CT Using Supervised Target-Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract: Quantitative assessment of infarct hypodensity on non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), including net water uptake (NWU), requires manual or semi-manual lesion delineation, often guided by CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI, limiting clinical applicability. Automated NCCT segmentation could enable such biomarker extraction but remains challenging across heterogeneous multicenter data. This study developed and externally tested a deep learning framework for ischemic stroke segmentation and NWU quantification on NCCT. In this retrospective multicenter study of 801 patients from four datasets, an nnU-Net-based model with foundation-model initialization, extended by modules comparing local features with the contralateral hemisphere, was trained on NCCT scans from the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf and the Acute Ischemic Stroke Dataset. The model was fine-tuned on target-domain subsets of the Boston (n=11) and ISLES (n=75) datasets, with evaluation on held-out cases. Segmentations and NWU were compared with expert references. Internally, mean Dice increased from 0.53 (conventional nnU-Net) to 0.57 (proposed approach). After fine-tuning, the proposed approach achieved median Dice of 0.56 for acute lesion segmentation (Boston) and 0.26 for post-treatment final-infarct prediction (ISLES), where small lesions predominated. For lesions >=30 mL, median Dice increased to 0.67 and 0.57, respectively. On the Boston dataset, automated and reference NWU agreed (concordance correlation coefficient 0.93, mean absolute error 1.24 percentage points). Contralateral feature comparison and target-domain adaptation supported NCCT-only infarct segmentation across heterogeneous external cohorts, although performance was lower for post-treatment final-infarct prediction. The approach enabled low-error NWU quantification from baseline NCCT without advanced imaging or manual annotation.

papers.title: RiskWorld: Risk-Aware World Modeling with Flow-Guided Occupancy Evolution for Selective Trajectory Planning in Automated Driving
papers.abstract: Safe motion planning in automated driving requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise the current planned trajectory. We introduce RiskWorld, a risk-aware world modeling framework for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement. Spatial risk fields and temporal actor context are fused with visual bird's-eye-view features. Flow-guided evolution transports occupancy and scene features, while signed residuals correct occupancy after transport. One forecast is generated per planning step and reused across candidates. Each candidate is compared with a current-state persistence reference, yielding a nonnegative collision-score correction. The trajectory selected by current-world evaluation serves as the planning anchor and is replaced only when additional predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative satisfies component-wise constraints on predicted risk and trajectory error. Candidate geometries remain unchanged. We evaluate RiskWorld for open-loop planning on nuScenes using camera features, annotation-derived current and historical actor states, and dataset-provided map context. RiskWorld achieves the lowest collision rate at a long evaluation horizon of 3 s, and the second-best average L2 error among various state-of-the-art baselines, while running at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 90.81 M parameters. Within-setting ablations show that RiskWorld achieves lower collision rates than the current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates to be evaluated at low marginal computational cost.

papers.title: Bad Genius: Counterfactual-Guided Harness Evolution Beyond Task-Specific Shortcuts
papers.abstract: An optimized agent harness can improve on held-out tasks by relying on formatting conventions that those tasks share with the rest of the benchmark. We introduce Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE) to test whether harness improvements survive changes to the evaluation protocol. A Proposer edits the harness around a fixed foundation model. A Challenger then searches for a protocol change that preserves the tasks but reduces the updated harness's gain over the initial harness. Executable checks test whether the transformation preserves task semantics. If the gain loss is confirmed on held-out tasks, CHASE adds the transformation to an archive that constrains subsequent harness updates. We give conditions under which this finite archive bounds the gain loss on an ideal benchmark with shortcuts removed. We evaluate CHASE on Syn-Ledger, OfficeQA, FinanceBench, and SWE-Bench Pro V2. On Syn-Ledger, removing the known shortcuts yields 38.30% accuracy for CHASE and 18.27% for HarnessEvolve. On the 21 certification tasks from SWE-Bench Pro V2 HARD-51, changing the issue formatting and tool-output field order reduces HarnessEvolve's gain over the initial harness from 8.57 to 3.81 percentage points. The final CHASE harness retains 10.48 points of its 11.43-point gain under the same change.

papers.title: $p$-ary (Non Weakly) Regular Bent Functions in Generalized $\cPS$ class
papers.abstract: We use $m$-dimensional partial spreads of $\fp^{2n}$, where $p$ is an odd prime, $n$ is a positive integer and $m$ divides $n$, to construct two classes of bent functions from $\fp^{2n}$ to $\fp$. Our construction generalizes the classes of $p$-ary $\cPS^{-}$ and $\cPS^{+}$ regular bent functions proposed by P. Lison\v ek and H. Y. Lu (Des. Codes Cryptogr. 73 (2014), 209--216). Unlike the original class, such bent functions can be either regular or non weakly regular.

papers.title: Landscape geometry of Majorana zero modes in inhomogeneous superconductors
papers.abstract: Conventional methods for characterizing Majorana zero modes in inhomogeneous superconductors generally cannot be applied directly when the potential profile is unknown. To address this limitation, we propose a real-space approach based on a landscape for the zero-energy spatial dynamics. The landscape geometry determines the number of Majorana zero modes, and the conventional topological phase transition is recovered as a geometric transition of the landscape in the homogeneous limit. Without specifying detailed spatial profiles, the approach yields analytical bounds on Hamiltonian parameters and their spatial gradients that guarantee Majorana zero modes. Application to nanowire--superconductor systems demonstrates the predictive power of this profile-independent criterion and quantifies tolerable electrostatic inhomogeneity for Majorana-device design. Landscape geometry thus offers a dynamical perspective with broad applicability to topological boundary states.

papers.title: SPROUT: The Open-Source Soft Growing Robot for Search and Rescue
papers.abstract: Soft robotic systems have long been theorized as ideal candidates for use in search and rescue operations; however, there have been significant barriers to entry in graduating soft robotic systems from the laboratory to the field. To address this gap in replicable, reliable soft robot systems, we present the designs for SPROUT, the Soft Pathfinding Robotic Observation Unit. The system has matured over years of interaction with professional urban search and rescue communities, with the goal of operating in dusty, wet, and isolated conditions. This manuscript contains supplementary material, including code, parts manifests, CAD assemblies, and build instructions to allow the broader robotics research community to build their own SPROUT systems. The modular hardware and ROS 2-based software stack support task-specific payloads and control functions, allowing SPROUT to be adapted for applications beyond search and rescue, including infrastructure inspection and archaeology. Here, we demonstrate SPROUT performing a variety of challenging inspection and traversal tasks in collapsed structure training sites used by first responders. The main project page is available online at https://sprout-mitll.github.io/sprout/.

papers.title: Cohomological Aspects of Entanglement Entropy: From Information Theory to Noncommutative Geometry
papers.abstract: We develop a cohomological framework for entanglement entropy that unifies information theory, operator algebras, and noncommutative geometry. Entropy is a 1-cocycle in information cohomology; we generalize this to the quantum setting via Hochschild and cyclic cohomology. For an inclusion of von Neumann algebras N contained in M with a faithful normal state w admitting a cyclic and separating vector, and a conditional expectation E: M -> N (whose existence is equivalent to modular invariance of N by Takesaki's theorem), we construct the entanglement complex as the image of the transgression map tau_w on the relative cyclic complex, where A is a dense *-subalgebra of M and B = A intersect N. Our main result identifies entanglement cohomology with the kernel of the restriction map HC*(A) -> HC*(B), up to the connecting homomorphism d of the long exact sequence of the pair (A,B); when d = 0, the identification is exact. The relative modular cocycle u_t = (Dw : D(w|_N) o E)_t generates explicit entanglement classes when E is not w-invariant, with the Araki relative entropy as its infinitesimal generator. The framework accommodates Type III von Neumann algebras, where no local density matrix exists, and leads to a holographic proposal: a subspace of H^1_ent is conjecturally dual to linearized modular Hamiltonian perturbations of the bulk entanglement wedge. We verify the construction in finite-dimensional, type II_1, and type III_1 examples.

papers.title: Impedance-Aware Optimized Pulse Patterns for Reconfigurable Battery Systems
papers.abstract: Reconfigurable battery systems (RBS) synthesize the converter output voltage by inserting and bypassing battery cell groups, so every switching state changes not only the source voltage but also the source impedance. This paper shows that this configuration-dependent impedance breaks a tacit assumption of optimized pulse patterns (OPP): patterns designed with the customary linear plant model overestimate their achievable current quality by up to an order of magnitude and converge to a distortion floor set by the resistance modulation. We propose impedance-aware optimized pulse patterns (IA-OPP), which embed the level-dependent source impedance in the optimization objective, combined with an event-budget formulation that treats the reconfiguration rate of the communication bus as a managed resource. An exact closed-form evaluation of the piecewise-exponential load current renders the objective smooth in the switching instants. In a simulated cascaded-bridge reference system, IA-OPP attains 0.52% current total harmonic distortion (THD) at a reconfiguration rate of 2.4 kHz, outperforming nearest-level modulation, phase-shifted carrier pulse-width modulation (PWM) at up to five times the switching rate, and a classical OPP baseline at every event budget; the advantage persists across the modulation-index range and under +-30% parameter mismatch. For three-wire star-connected systems, masking triplen orders in the objective restores the full advantage, with the impedance-aware patterns beating their linear-model counterparts by about 20% at equal budget.

papers.title: Feasible Search Behavior
papers.abstract: Consider a situation wherein a decision maker sequentially searches for the best alternative among heterogeneous options with an arbitrary search order. The agent partially learns the value of an option when inspecting it. The information structure jointly determines the ex-ante and ex-post value of investigating each option, thereby shaping the entire learning path. We characterize the set of all search behaviors compatible with some information structure, which forms a polytope. A single information structure rationalizes all these search behaviors, which minimizes the agent's welfare among all information structures. Under certain symmetry assumption over primitives, we also examine the set of all feasible pairs of search and choice behaviors, with and without option sellers' price competition, and prove the same results. Our study not only provides a simple framework for analyzing how information shapes ordered learning paths, but also offers sharp insights into information design and identification problems in such environments.

papers.title: Edge observables in Maxwell theory on null boundaries
papers.abstract: We study edge observables in three-dimensional Maxwell theory on null boundaries using a Hamiltonian formulation adapted to null foliations. We consider three backgrounds: Minkowski spacetime, the BTZ black hole, and de Sitter space, where the relevant boundaries are, respectively, null infinity, the black hole horizon, and the cosmological horizon. In all three cases we find, besides the usual $\mathrm U(1)$ charge, a second edge observable associated with a shift transformation intrinsic to the null boundary. The two charges are well defined quasilocally. They form a centrally extended algebra which, in Fourier modes, becomes two independent Abelian Kac--Moody algebras with opposite levels. Thus, the same centrally extended edge structure appears at both asymptotic and finite distance null boundaries. The phase space also admits charge-conjugation twisted configurations, in which the modes of the algebra are half-integer. Finally, in Minkowski spacetime we find an exact radiative solution in this twisted sector, with both charges nonvanishing.

papers.title: Nonparametric Regression on Fixed-Cardinality Subsets:Minimax Risk and Random-Design Effects
papers.abstract: We study regression from noisy evaluations of uniformly sampled subsets containing exactly \(k\) items from a ground set of size \(d\), a setting motivated by combination screening. The fixed-cardinality constraint couples membership coordinates and prevents a direct use of product-domain notions of interaction and smoothness. Using the harmonic decomposition of the Johnson graph, we define an intrinsic Johnson--Sobolev scale and determine the exact dimensions of low-order interaction spaces. We establish finite-sample risk bounds for harmonic projection and a nonasymptotic minimax characterization when the Sobolev energy budget is bounded relative to the noise variance proxy. We also study sparsity when responses depend on few items, quantifying the reduced interaction dimension and the effects of unknown support and rare configurations. When the empirical Gram matrix is well conditioned, stable least squares removes the design fluctuation of the component already in the fitted space. A rank-deficiency analysis identifies the components left unresolved by random sampling. Combined with a centered completion estimator, it yields minimax bounds matching up to constants whenever \(\min(k,d-k)\) and the smoothness order are fixed, without restricting the signal-to-noise ratio. Numerical experiments distinguish observation noise, design fluctuation, and incomplete coverage; NCI-ALMANAC drug-pair scores provide a real-data illustration.

papers.title: PHP decompositions and primitivity of group rings
papers.abstract: We show that every countable group $G$ that has Ozawa's property $\rm PHP$ and contains a non-abelian free subgroup has the following property: the group ring $KG$ is primitive for any field $K$. As a consequence, we greatly extend the previously existing results on the primitivity of group rings. New examples include linear groups and groups of homeomorphisms of the Cantor set. Along the way, we prove that the class of groups with $\rm PHP$ enjoys some permanence properties that are of independent interest.

papers.title: NAQsim: Full-Stack Architecture Simulation Framework for Fast and Space-Efficient Neutral Atom Quantum Computing
papers.abstract: Technological advances in neutral-atom platforms have opened a new path toward designing efficient protocols for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). However, each physical operation is still orders of magnitude slower than on other platforms, such as superconducting qubits. Therefore, architects must identify fast and efficient FTQC architectures, which require reliable modeling tools to explore various design choices across the software, classical hardware, and quantum device stacks of neutral-atom platforms. In this paper, we propose NAQsim, an open-source simulation framework for neutral-atom FTQC architectures based on transversal gates. As its key feature, NAQsim enables detailed full-stack architecture evaluation that opens opportunities to explore previously overlooked performance bottlenecks. As a first use case for NAQsim, we identify one such bottleneck, patch rotations, perform full-stack co-optimization, and finally derive a near-rotation-free architecture (D3-ROT). For practical FTQC benchmark workloads, D3-ROT achieves a 2.27x speedup from this single bottleneck alone, with minimal footprint overhead. These results point to a much broader space of full-stack optimizations that NAQsim makes accessible for transversal surface-code architectures and beyond.

papers.title: Synthetic Leprosy Image Generation Using Mask-Conditioned Latent Diffusion and Transfer Learning from Large Chronic Wound Datasets
papers.abstract: Machine learning for neglected tropical diseases is limited by data, not algorithms: public annotated image sets for leprosy (Hansen's disease) number in the hundreds. We ask whether a model trained on abundant chronic wound photography transfers to this low-data regime. We build a three-stage pipeline: a DeepLabV3-ResNet50 segmenter supplies lesion masks for two wound datasets that ship without them; a mask-conditioned latent diffusion model built from Stable Diffusion 1.5 components is trained on 3,280 wound crops; and the model is fine-tuned on leprosy image-mask pairs from CO2Wounds-V2 (764 images of 96 patients). We evaluate on 136 held-out leprosy lesions using LPIPS anchored by a real-versus-real baseline, kernel inception distance (KID), and a paired design that runs both models on the same input. Fine-tuning moved the generated distribution toward real held-out leprosy images: KID fell from 0.167 to 0.089, and LPIPS distance to real images from 0.806 to 0.765, with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals. Giving the base model the leprosy prompt alone did not reproduce the gain (KID 0.250). For a fixed input, fine-tuning changes the output less than a new random seed does (paired LPIPS 0.544 versus 0.728): it keeps layout and alters tissue color and texture. The generated set shows no mode collapse (internal diversity 0.734 versus 0.667 for real images). A dataset audit shows that a majority of training images carry synthetic flat regions from preprocessing, which the fine-tuned model partly reproduces. Chronic wound photography is a viable donor domain for leprosy lesion synthesis; the remaining barrier is semantic control rather than image quality.

papers.title: A weighted restriction estimate in $\mathbb R^2$
papers.abstract: We establish a weighted restriction estimate in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Our proof combines new two-ends Furstenberg estimates with refined decoupling.As an application, our result yields decay estimates for the circular $L^p$-means of the Fourier transforms of fractal measures in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

papers.title: Morphology-Aware Human Motion Retargeting for Wheeled-Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: We propose a whole-body teleoperation method for topology-mismatched humanoids, with a focus on motion retargeting and whole-body control for wheeled humanoids. First, we design a Topology-Adaptive Motion Retargeting (TAMR) method with a robust switching logic that selects mapping joints according to human posture. Second, we train a Teacher-Student DAgger method that supports real-time teleoperation with inertial motion capture and virtual-reality devices. We further develop a Temporal Feasibility-Aware Command Governor (T-FeaCG) for the wheeled base to reduce the mismatch between teleoperation policy intent and the feasible execution margin of a three-steer-wheel base. We will release the complete teleoperation code and dataset, and demonstrate whole-body humanoid skills learned from teleoperation. More videos are available at: https://xiachenbuo.github.io/Morphology-Aware-Human-Motion-Retargeting-for-Wheeled-Humanoid-Loco-Manipulation/.

papers.title: Are You Learning Biological Signal or Shortcuts? Auditing and Mitigating Bias in Protein-Protein Interaction Datasets
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) databases do not faithfully reflect biological realities. Instead, they are influenced by study and technical biases that distort certain protein and interaction attributes. Machine learning models can exploit these as learning shortcuts if the negative dataset is not constructed with care. So far, the shortcuts introduced during PPI dataset construction have only been examined in isolation. Here, we systematically characterize both reported and, to our knowledge, previously unreported biases in PPI datasets that lead machine learning models to learn shortcuts instead of biological signal. We analyze HIPPIE, IntAct, and STRING, dedicated PPI databases, as well as two datasets derived from 3D-structural information in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We show that random data splitting introduces strong topological shortcuts. When train-test protein overlap is removed, the resulting datasets still retain usable shortcuts stemming from self-interactions, taxonomic identity, and functional relatedness, whose prevalence interestingly depends on the data source. We further show that sampling negatives from a set of highly replicated non-interactions, an intuitively appealing choice, can amplify the shortcut stemming from functional relatedness. To detect and mitigate these biases, we provide an open Nextflow pipeline that combines similarity-aware, data-loss-minimizing dataset splitting with bias-minimizing negative sampling, both formulated as integer linear programs. Its key concept of quantifying biases to minimize them through optimization-based negative sampling can, in principle, be extended to any machine learning problem where the pool of negative candidates is much larger than the positives and is thus of interest also beyond PPI prediction.

papers.title: Multiparameter quantum bounds for entanglement-assisted aperture synthesis
papers.abstract: Entanglement-assisted optical interferometry promises diffraction-limited imaging over baselines where light cannot be physically combined, but its estimation-theoretic bounds exist only for a single visibility on one baseline. This work formulates the multiparameter quantum estimation problem for an M-station array. A reduction lemma shows that the multimode quantum Fisher information (QFI) equals the mean photon number times the QFI of a single delocalized photon, making the problem finite-dimensional. The local photon-number superselection rule erases all phase information from the bare state; shared entanglement restores a fraction f(r)=r/(1+r) of the QFI on a baseline supplied with r pairs, a benchmark that applies to every pair of the array. The QFI matrix and its mean Uhlmann curvature show numerically that a point source is measurement-compatible, whereas every extended-source model examined is incompatible; a semidefinite-programming evaluation shows that the Holevo bound exceeds the symmetric-logarithmic-derivative bound by up to ~24% for three stations and by 4-8% for larger arrays and for CHARA. An explicit collective receiver, a numerically optimised global linear-optical network with photon counting, attains a weighted variance within 2-9% of the Holevo bound, over an order of magnitude below an explicit pairwise receiver, and a noisy-resource threshold gives the break-even baseline (~22 km for illustrative parameters) beyond which distributed entanglement beats direct transmission. Finally, allocating a finite entanglement budget has a closed-form proportional (square-root-law) solution for a per-baseline fringe cost, whereas for the source-parameter variance under an explicit photon budget the routing of photons matters far more than the entanglement split. These results recast quantum aperture synthesis as collective multiparameter estimation, illustrated on CHARA.

papers.title: Logarithmic Stability for an Inverse Source Problem in a Coupled Nonlinear Helmholtz System
papers.abstract: We consider an inverse source problem for a coupled nonlinear Helmholtz system motivated by second-harmonic generation. For a known susceptibility bounded away from zero, we prove that small real-valued sources are uniquely determined by the full first Fréchet derivative of the nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann map at a fixed small real boundary value. Under an a priori Sobolev bound, we derive a conditional logarithmic stability estimate. The proof uses linearization, complex geometric optics solutions for a matrix Schrödinger equation, and interpolation.

papers.title: TabBench-Bio: A Living Benchmark for Machine Learning on High-Dimensional Biomedical Tables
papers.abstract: Biomedical tables often combine thousands of measured variables with only tens or hundreds of labelled samples, a regime that is poorly represented in general-purpose tabular benchmarks. We introduce TabBench-Bio, a living and interactive benchmark of 43 biomedical datasets spanning multiple domains. Under a shared cross-validation protocol, we compare classical estimators, neural networks, and tabular foundation models across 28 feature-by-sample operating points. At the reference cell of 10,000 features and 100 training samples, RealTabPFN 2.5 has the highest point estimate, closely followed by TabPFN 3 and Logistic Regression. A paired bootstrap over the target pool separates RealTabPFN 2.5 from TabPFN 3 by 87 Elo (95\% interval [43, 129]). Tabular foundation models generally occupy the leading ranks, while the strongest configuration depends on the operating point and biomedical modality. The AutoML framework AutoGluon, using its one-hour "extreme" preset, is configured as a separate resource-intensive reference and reported here at the reference and full cell. Fold-level predictions, run status, and deterministic aggregations make every reported result reproducible and reusable. The benchmark is open to contributions of new biomedical datasets. The interactive leaderboard is available at https://tabbench-bio.eu.

papers.title: An Outer Giant Excites and Constrains the Orbit of $π$ Mensae d
papers.abstract: The nearby $π$ Mensae system contains the eccentric giant planet b on a 5.7 yr orbit, the 6.27 day transiting sub-Neptune c, and a candidate planet d on a 123 day orbit between them. Published estimates place the eccentricity of d between approximately 0.2 and 0.4. We reanalyze 772 published velocities with three-Keplerian fits and explore three-dimensional b-d dynamics with $N$-body integrations. The high-eccentricity solution persists when the phase or apsidal prior is widened; exact importance reweighting to a population-informed Beta eccentricity prior gives $e_d=0.378^{+0.050}_{-0.049}$. In 20 kyr integrations, 84.5% of configurations near the prograde and retrograde coplanar endpoints survive, compared with 21.3% across $60^\circ\leq I_{bd}<120^\circ$; stellar collisions dominate the failures. Secular forcing by b moves 53 of 62 one-Myr survivors initialized with $e_d\leq0.1$ into $0.3\leq e_d\leq0.5$. Representative b+d configurations remain viable for 100 Myr, whereas controls with c and general relativity retain fewer systems. The outer giant can therefore excite the observed eccentricity of d while constraining its viable orbit toward prograde or retrograde near-coplanar configurations.

papers.title: OracleZoom: Reference-Constrained Recursive Image Super-Resolution Beyond Ground Truth
papers.abstract: Recursive image Super-Resolution (SR) reaches extreme magnification by feeding each prediction back into the same model, like zooming into an image again and again. Real ground truth for deep zooms is impractical to capture (a full $256\times$ target would be a 52 GB image), so predictions at deeper zooms have no supervision. Yet the last ground-truth image still contains the region that every deeper zoom magnifies. OracleZoom turns this region into a training signal. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation, the model trains on its own prediction for one recursive step ($4\times \rightarrow 16\times$), and a cross-scale loss projects each $16\times$ prediction back to the last ground truth at $4\times$. This projection can verify only coarse content, so a no-reference quality objective guides the remaining fine detail, and a latent prior stops this objective from adding hallucinated artifacts. On seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves the highest CLIPIQA at every zoom depth (mean 0.713 vs. 0.621 for Chain-of-Zoom), with the largest gains at the deepest zooms, even though training stops at $16\times$ and optimizes a different quality metric. Pooled over two ground-truth-anchored judges, this added detail comes at the same hallucination rate as Chain-of-Zoom at $16\times$ and a lower rate at $4\times$, and removing the cross-scale loss raises hallucination at $16\times$.

papers.title: Quantum information spreading via higher-order operator correlators
papers.abstract: We provide an exact analytical benchmarks into measuring the quantum information spreading by introducing N-operator correlators. Leveraging the idea from N-point correlation function from cosmology, we formulate a generalized Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlator (OTOC), called N-Operator Correlator (NOC). Such formulation can reduce the effect of restricted analysis associated with selecting only two operators for OTOC. NOC can take into account a larger set of measurement probes in measuring the degree of quantum information spreading. We demonstrate these concepts with two analytically tractable systems with computing thermal averages of operator time evolutions at a finite temperature: a single qubit in longitudinal field and isotropic XXX model with a transverse field, two-qubit system. Our analytical benchmark serves as a basic introduction to generalized operator correlators in quantum mechanics.

papers.title: Two Principles for Autoregressive Language Modeling
papers.abstract: We investigate the functional differentiation learned by RoPE Transformers to derive principles for autoregressive language modeling. We introduce two intervention-based metrics: RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS) measures how removing a frequency contribution changes a head's full attention distribution, and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD) isolates the effect of rotary modulation. In Qwen3 and Llama3.1, these metrics distinguish retrieval from positional modeling, while individual heads can exhibit both functions. A mid-low-frequency Global Positional Band (GPBand) separates their frequency dependencies and tracks the training sequence length in controlled experiments, suggesting that global positional fitting can hinder zero-shot length extrapolation. These findings motivate two principles. (1) Functional Organization: retrieval and positional functions should be assigned separately and mixed within layers with layer-specific allocation; and (2) Positional Dependence: positional modeling should operate only locally, while global access should rely on position-independent retrieval. Matched pretraining from scratch and targeted architectural ablations at 380M and 1.4B parameters support both principles and highlight the importance of mechanism choice in realizing each function. Together, these findings suggest a promising route toward architectural innovation grounded in the functional requirements of autoregressive language modeling.

papers.title: Adelic points and unmramified Brauer approximation for classifying stacks
papers.abstract: Let $k$ be a number field. We study adelic topologies and strong approximation for classifying stacks. For a connected linear algebraic group $G$, we relate the Brauer-Manin obstruction on $BG$ to Kottwitz's localisation sequence and identify the quotient of the unramified Brauer group of $BG$ by the Brauer group of $k$ with the cyclic Tate-Shafarevich group of the character module of $G$. This yields a local criterion for strong approximation with respect to the unramified Brauer group. Finally, for an abelian variety $A$, we compute the cohomological Brauer group of $BA$ and show that, when the group of $k$-rational points on the dual abelian variety has positive rank, strong approximation with respect to the full Brauer group fails off every finite set of places.

papers.title: Frequency-domain extended-effective-source gravitational self-force for eccentric Schwarzschild orbits
papers.abstract: Effective-source formulations provide a practical route to gravitational self-force (GSF) calculations when singular retarded fields cannot be handled directly mode by mode. Before this work, frequency-domain effective-source calculations of the first-order GSF had been performed only for circular Schwarzschild orbits. We construct and implement a frequency-domain extended effective-source (EES) formulation for first-order Lorenz-gauge GSF on eccentric orbits in Schwarzschild spacetime. The central obstacle is that radial libration forces the physical puncture and effective source to switch between interior and exterior branches, limiting their differentiability and producing slow spectral convergence. We overcome this obstruction by analytically extending both branches across the libration region and solving the coupled Lorenz-gauge perturbation equations for the resulting smooth extended sources. This provides an end-to-end gravitational EES implementation for eccentric motion and validates a computational ingredient needed for extending frequency-domain effective-source calculations toward second order.

papers.title: Adapting a Foundation Model for Lunar Surface Height Estimation
papers.abstract: Digital elevation models (DEMs) can provide accurate height information, making it invaluable for analyzing the lunar surface. Due to recent advancements in computer vision, the focus is on generating DEMs using monocular depth estimation via deep learning. Classic lunar crater detection methods rely mainly on 2D image data. Our goal is to address this issue by developing a relative lunar surface height estimator that could provide additional information for crater localization. In this letter, we present a methodology that builds on the zero-shot relative depth estimation model Depth Anything V2 (DAV2). Other works have been using it as a state-of-the-art comparison for their proposed lunar DEM estimation method, but without adaptations to the target domain. Thus, it may underperform. Therefore, we propose a fine-tuning strategy with publicly available SPG-derived DEM data of the lunar surface, and refer to it as DEM-DAV2. Specifically, we introduce new learnable parameters in the Transformer-based encoder with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), and we unfreeze certain layers in the model's decoder. On our test set, the proposed DEM-DAV2 reduces the average MAE and RMSE by $\sim$80\% and $\sim$79\%, respectively, compared to the zero-shot DAV2. This demonstrates a significant improvement in performance compared to the zero-shot model, effectively transforming DAV2 into a reliable relative height estimator of the lunar surface. However, the predictions remain relative and require scale recovery from a low-resolution DEM such as SLDEM.

papers.title: RadMatch: Auditable Radiology Report Evaluation via Finding-Level Matching
papers.abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to draft radiology reports, reliably evaluating their clinical quality remains a critical challenge. We introduce RadMatch, a multi-stage LLM-based framework that turns report evaluation into a structured, auditable finding-level record. It extracts findings from a reference and a candidate report, matches them by clinical equivalence, grades each match over ten clinical attributes, and gives every match and unmatched finding a verdict and a clinical-significance tier. To validate metrics on CT, we build and release MetricEval-BodyCT, the first public metric-evaluation benchmark of chest and abdomen CT reports annotated by radiologists error by error. On it and three chest X-ray benchmarks, RadMatch with an open 31B judge on consumer GPUs agrees with radiologists more closely than previous published metrics, and even reaches inter-expert agreement on ReXVal and on the significant errors of MetricEval-BodyCT. Radiologists auditing its decisions on 60 studies confirm 98.5% of its matches and 93.6% of the errors it counts. When used to evaluate state-of-the-art radiology report generation models, RadMatch shows that most CT models, unlike several chest X-ray models, actually leave more significant errors than an image-blind normal template, as their added unsupported findings outnumber the reference findings they correctly report. We provide RadMatch's code, its dashboard, the MetricEval-BodyCT dataset and all per-report scores.

papers.title: Autonomous discovery of new structure-plausibility laws for explainable and rapid crystal diagnosis and screening
papers.abstract: Generative models and autonomous agents now propose candidate inorganic crystals by the million, yet most screens test little beyond a minimum-distance cutoff and give no chemical reason for failure. For nearly a century, Pauling's rules have served as the main empirical theory of crystal-structure stability, but they remain qualitative and idealized, leading to only 6.5% of known ionic crystals satisfying rules 2--5 simultaneously. Here our agents generate, test and refute two million candidate laws to discover eight Plausibility Rules for Inorganic Structures (PRIS). These laws encode five physical mechanisms: short-range repulsion, ionic contact and packing, electrostatic balance, bond-valence conservation and crystallographic site simplicity. Experimental structures satisfy the PRIS law sets in 82--99% of cases, and the strictest set detects 87.9% of artificially damaged structures, far above the 1.6--3.2% of conventional distance cutoffs. Although derived without synthesis labels, PRIS plausibility is highly linearly correlated with synthesizability, and a continuous PRIS-derived synthesis score (PSS) explainably filters out 83.7% of hard-to-synthesize structures while retaining 80.7% of experimental structures. In an inverse-design task targeting ultra-incompressible crystals, explainable screening by PRIS and PSS cuts the density functional theory (DFT) validation queue by up to 67.3% while retaining 99.2% of the DFT-verified target candidates. Beyond screening, PRIS traces GNoME's low-symmetry excess to artificial element ordering and identifies falsified crystal structures. PRIS moves screening from a pass-or-fail verdict to a chemical reason for failure, showing that autonomous agents can discover, by active refutation, physicochemical laws that guide calculations and experiments.

papers.title: Ceiling-Clipped Acceptance Histograms Indicate Stranded Speed-up in Block-Diffusion Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up generation using an efficient draft model (drafter) to propose tokens that a target model verifies in one pass, preserving the target's output distribution. High-acceptance block-diffusion drafters, such as DFlash and DFlare, fill an entire block in one parallel pass. In many cycles, the target model accepts all draft tokens in the block, so the drafter exhausts its trained horizon before verification ever fails. We call this unrealized acceptance stranded speed-up. Evaluating a drafter by its per-prompt or per-cycle mean committed length alone hides this phenomenon, whereas the acceptance histogram exposes this bottleneck as a spike in the ceiling bin, the fraction of cycles that accept the entire block. We recommend reviewing the acceptance histogram before spending more training compute. Naively widening the block at inference could reduce acceptance for drafters with bidirectional attention, since, once the block outgrows its training size, the drafter's bidirectional attention shifts its distribution even at early positions, which empirically degrades acceptance there. We therefore post-train the drafter to a longer block with a short curriculum that emphasizes the newly exposed positions, a method we call DBloom. We continue training the pretrained DFlash and DFlare drafters at the original block size of 16, before expanding them to 24 (B16 to B24) on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B. Compared to the original B16 drafters, this technique raises per-prompt committed length by up to +1.7 tokens and decode speed-up by a median of +10.2% versus +5.7% without the continuation. On high-ceiling benchmarks, the speed-up rises to +11.9%. On Gemma-4-12B-IT and GPT-OSS-20B, expansion also raises committed length on every benchmark. Against JetSpec, a tree drafter, DBloom has higher committed length by point estimate on every benchmark at tree budgets up to 64 nodes.

papers.title: Spin-dependent fermion potentials from mixed tensor couplings of massive spin-1 and spin-2 bosons
papers.abstract: Searches for weak spin-dependent forces are commonly interpreted in terms of a basis of sixteen rotationally invariant two-fermion potentials. We derive finite-range coordinate-space potentials generated by a massive spin-1 boson with vector, axial-vector, tensor, and pseudotensor couplings to Dirac fermions. In addition to the familiar vector--vector, vector--axial-vector, and axial-vector--axial-vector interactions, we obtain the mixed vector--tensor, vector--pseudotensor, axial-vector--tensor, and axial-vector--pseudotensor potentials, together with tensor--tensor, tensor--pseudotensor, and pseudotensor--pseudotensor terms. We retain the contact terms needed in atomic-scale applications and give compact expressions that include both orderings of inequivalent fermion vertices. We then extend the analysis to a massive spin-2 mediator described by a symmetric Fierz--Pauli field. Besides the conventional coupling to the conserved fermion energy--momentum tensor, we consider a symmetric axial-tensor current. Its nonconservation for massive fermions makes the longitudinal spin-2 helicities contribute to axial-tensor--axial-tensor exchange. The leading minimal spin-2 interactions are either P,T even or P odd and T evenl. Heavy-mediator contact limits and the distinction between the M-->0 massive-spin-2 limit and a genuine massless graviton are also discussed. We map the resulting interactions onto the sixteen-potential Dobrescu--Mocioiu basis and use this mapping to translate existing experimental constraints into numerical limits on spin-1 and spin-2 coupling products in the small- and large-mediator-mass regimes, together with representative limits at finite mediator masses. The derived relations between the boson-exchange coupling constants and the coefficients of the basis potentials also allow published exclusion curves to be rescaled to arbitrary mediator masses.

papers.title: MAP: A Benchmark on Multimodal Accessibility Planning for Real World Places
papers.abstract: We introduce MAP, the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal AI systems as assistants for users with accessibility requirements when planning visits to places in the real world. In our evaluation, systems are presented with requests to verify or recommend a point of interest meeting an accessibility requirement. MAP contains two novel assessments: Claim verification for accessibility planning assesses if information on places and stated accessibility features is supported and identifies places that satisfy requested accessibility features. Visual evidence retrieval for accessibility planning checks if a multimodal AI system can select visual evidence for the requested place and accessibility feature. Our methodology supports comparison of AI systems in a setting where place information and accessibility information can change over time by evaluating systems and refreshing ground truth data at scheduled times. The benchmark is based on automatic rating and human rating for a proportion of responses.

papers.title: Visual Token Coding for Video Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a new token compression paradigm for video Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), termed Visual Token Coding ($VTC$). Inspired by classical video coding principles, e.g., HEVC, VTC performs structured compression by predicting the I/P frames of a video and measuring their frame-wise residuals to estimate token redundancy. Based on this base paradigm, we further extend VTC with a set of dynamic budgeting designs towards more cost-effective token coding, termed $VTC_{dy}$. To validate VTC and $VTC_{dy}$, we apply them to three MLLMs and conduct experiments on a set of video understanding benchmarks. The experimental results show that as a base paradigm, VTC can achieve an average performance retention of 98.4% on Qwen3-VL under a 50% token compression ratio, and the enhanced $VTC_{dy}$ can further improve the retention to 100.3%, outperforming a set of compared methods. Moreover, as a plug-and-play design, VTC requires no additional tuning of MLLMs for token coding. Our code is given in the supplementary materials.

papers.title: How do features act in an individual prediction? Separating standalone and interaction effects with a case-based taxonomy
papers.abstract: Local explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME summarize each feature with a single attribution score, and interaction indices quantify how strongly features interact. Neither tells a user how a feature acts in a given prediction: whether its effect is the same alone and in context, or whether the other features amplify it, make it unnecessary, switch it off or reverse it. We extend case-based feature importance (CBFI), originally a global method, to individual predictions. Evaluating the model in four hybrid states per background sample decomposes the in-context importance of a feature into a standalone and an interaction effect, and a case taxonomy labels each feature of an instance as inactive, standalone, amplified, redundant, gated or reversed. We compare the method with k-SII, TreeSHAP interaction values and the H-statistic on synthetic functions, and study eight real tabular datasets with six model families. On the true functions, the decomposition recovered interactions exactly (correlation 0.99 with the analytic local interaction). On fitted models, pair recovery was slightly below that of dedicated indices (local precision@k 0.86-0.91 versus 0.91-0.95). Interaction values alone could not distinguish substitution from gating, whereas the taxonomy identified both without knowing the partner (accuracy 0.74-0.76); applied to Shapley interaction values, it performed comparably. On real data, 45-57% of feature pairs with nearly identical SHAP values received different labels, and in a medical-insurance model the method showed that the interaction component of smoking changes sign at a body-mass index of 30. Localized CBFI does not detect interactions more accurately than existing indices; what it adds is a decomposition into standalone and interaction effects and a label stating how each feature acts.

papers.title: Video-OPSD: Exploiting Privileged Visual Evidence for On-Policy Self-Distillation in Video Large Language Models
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has recently emerged as an effective post-training paradigm that provides dense token-level supervision from a privileged self-teacher, yet it remains underexplored for Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs). Existing methods typically construct privileged teachers by augmenting their context with additional information while keeping the primary input unchanged for both teacher and student. In video reasoning, however, privileged information can also be found within the primary input itself: videos contain substantial temporal redundancy, and only a few frames carry the evidence needed to answer a question. Building on this observation, we present $\textbf{Video-OPSD}$, an OPSD framework that exploits privileged visual evidence for both self-teacher construction and knowledge transfer. First, our Evidence-Grounded Self-Teacher conditions the teacher exclusively on annotated evidence frames, while the student reasons over a broader set of frames that contains them. This focused visual context enables more targeted supervision without introducing visual content unavailable to the student. Second, our Evidence-Guided Token Optimization adaptively weights token-level distillation according to an estimate of each reasoning token's reliance on privileged visual evidence, thereby emphasizing perceptually grounded reasoning. Across five video benchmarks and three Qwen-VL backbones, $\textbf{Video-OPSD}$ consistently outperforms Standard OPSD by 1.8-2.3 percentage points on average, establishing an effective and efficient post-training approach for Video-LLMs.

papers.title: MVC-Bench: Benchmarking Calibration of Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Reliable evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) and medical vision-language models (Medical-VLMs) requires calibrated confidence, particularly under realistic clinical conditions. However, existing efforts mainly focused on improving accuracy, leaving calibration in the medical domain underexplored. To this end, we propose MVC-Bench, a calibration-centric benchmark for medical image classification with VLMs and Medical-VLMs. MVC-Bench assesses the calibration across three axes: (i) robustness to modality, backbone, and domain shift (ii) effectiveness of calibration strategies and prompt-tuning methods (iii) stability under prompt-template and random-seed variations. The benchmark covers eight different backbones, three medical modalities, including fundus imaging, histopathology, and chest X-ray under in-domain and domain shift settings. It compares post-hoc calibration, train-time calibration, and zero-shot inference methods, together with six prompt-tuning methods. Across more than 1638 controlled experiments, we report accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as primary metrics, and further report results with complementary calibration measures, including Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) and Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE). We further investigate the underlying causes of miscalibration in VLMs and Medical-VLMs and propose a simple train-time calibration method, Multi-Class Margin (MCM) regularization, which achieves lowest ECE on 10 out of 12 settings in in-domain and remains competitive under domain shifts. Collectively, MVC-Bench provides a structured evaluation framework and actionable guidance for improving calibration in safety-critical medical workflows.

papers.title: Language Model Security Modules: Turning LLM Interpretability into Runtime Defense
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are served behind layered defenses such as alignment and guardrail models, yet jailbreaks still get through. Interpretability research looks inside the model, where methods such as probes and sparse autoencoders expose signals of harmful content during generation. A signal alone, however, is not a defense. To become one, the serving system must tie each signal to the right request, apply the policy as declared, and release output only when the policy allows. Today, defenses built on such signals handle these duties on their own, so every new detector needs its own integration. Yet none of these duties depends on how a signal is computed.
